newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: New S.Korean law to help N.Korean defectors cope.
newsitem.headline: New S.Korean law to help N.Korean defectors cope.

text.p: South Korea, faced with a growing number of defections from the communist North, adopted new legislation on Monday to help asylum seekers cope with their new capitalist home.
The centrepiece of the new law is a half-way house where defectors will spend their first year studying politics, the economy, culture and social studies.

Another two years will be spent easing the new arrivals into society, with the government offering subsidised education and housing, as well as job training. During this time, they will be under police supervision.
The entire programme will be administered by the Ministry of National Unification instead of a previous cluster of government agencies.
"We needed a systematic way to re-educate defectors as about half of them seemed to be having trouble adapting to their new environment," said the official, who declined to be identified.
The government will fund the initial year of re-education.
The South is hoping to open a re-education centre by November next year with places for 100 people. Eventually, the facility will expand to house 500 defectors.
Each defector will be eligible for up to 31.6 million won (US$35,000) in assistance.

Cash payments will be made to the small number of military personnel who arrive with military hardware and government officials who flee their Stalinist homeland with secrets. Previously awards were also offered in gold.

A fighter jet or naval vessel is worth up to 150 million won, any other kind of aircraft 50 million won, a tank 50 million won, side arms and rifles 10 million won. Secrets are valued at up to 250 million won.
It was not clear whether the new law would be applied retroactively to include defector Hwang Jang-yop, North Korea's former ideology tsar who arrived in April.
Hwang has warned that hunger-stricken North Korea, its economy in ruins, is preparing to invade South Korea out of desperation.
But the law is mainly aimed at helping the vast majority of defectors who arrive with nothing but the clothes on their backs.

Currently 651 North Koreans reside in South Korea, with 195 of them having arrived since 1994. Already this year, 52 defectors have come to Seoul, and increasingly whole families have been escaping the impoverished North.
North Korean watchers say the number will only increase as the Stalinist state faces a looming famine.

While some defectors welcomed the new legislation, others said it was still far behind a law used before 1993 that considered defectors as national heroes, gave them larger sums of relocation funds and posted them with private companies that were obliged to give them work.

But the 1993 law ended most of these provisions and defectors had to scramble to find jobs, usually ending up pumping gas or working at construction sites, according to a defector who came to Korea more than 30 years ago.

"The one year education programme will be helpful for North Korean escapees, and I'm sure the defectors will be better managed after the programme as well," said another defector, Han Tae-suk, who is president of a group for defectors in Seoul. ($1 = 890 won)
